newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden launches new investigation into Nazi gold.
newsitem.headline: Sweden launches new investigation into Nazi gold.

text.p: Sweden's central bank said on Wednesday it would launch a new investigation next month into Nazi gold bought by Sweden during World War Two in the wake of fresh allegations.

The Swedish daily Dagens Nyheter reported this week that Sweden may have used up to seven tonnes of gold bought from Nazi Germany during World War Two despite suspicions that perhaps two-thirds of it may have been stolen.
"This new report shows that there may still be documents we have not noticed," the central bank's legal counsellor, Robert Sparve, told Reuters.
"We want to make sure we have not missed anything."
Sweden's policy during the war has come under scrutiny following criticism of Swiss banks' dealings with Nazi Germany.

Both countries were neutral during the war but Sweden maintained extensive trade ties with Germany, selling large amounts of iron ore in return for gold that some historians now say may have been looted from Jews or from occupied countries.
Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, carried out an investigation last autumn to check whether any of the gold bullion held in Swedish vaults originated from Nazi Germany.
"We found no significant connection with the gold the Riksbank acquired from Germany during the war," Sparve said.
But he said the new investigation, due to start in mid-February, would concentrate on the bank's archives to establish whether any relevant information had been overlooked.
The bank has appointed three external lawyers, headed by former Supreme Court judge Jan Heuman, to carry out an investigation expected to take about six months.
The latest revelations claim the Swedish wartime government put pressure on the central bank not to ask too many questions about the origins of gold emanating from Nazi Germany.

The latest report said Riksbank governor Ivar Rooth expressed concern to Trade Minister Herman Eriksson in February 1943 about allied threats to demand post-war compensation if it was shown that neutral governments had bought looted Nazi gold.
The trade minister said in two separate memos that Rooth should not concern himself with the origins of the German gold.
Another memo urged Rooth to do his outmost to meet Germany's requests for more gold trade.
Germany subsequently reassured Sweden that the gold it was using for payment was not looted, a statement used frequently for the rest of the war to justify continued Swedish purchases.
Sweden returned about 13 tonnes of gold to Belgium and the Netherlands after the war when it was shown it had been looted by occupying Germans.

Sweden only decided in March 1944, a year before the end of the war and months before allied troops launched the invasion of France, to stop accepting German gold in return for the 35 million tonnes of Swedish iron ore.
